results.question: You receive two Visa card offers: Option A is free but charges 1.5% on every foreign transaction. Option B costs CHF 8/month but has zero foreign fees. You travel to Europe 2–3 times a year. Which do you pick and why?
results.answer:
I'd choose Option A, the free one. Honestly, even though I travel a couple of times a year, the few transactions I make abroad wouldn't amount to enough to justify paying CHF 96 annually for Option B. Plus, my Twint app already handles most of my daily needs without any extra charges, so I'd rather stick with what I know and save that CHF 8 each month. It adds up over time! [/ANS] 

The best answer is A[/ANS]

results.question: Your bank sends you a message: your free debit card will be replaced by a new Visa card at CHF 5/month. You can opt out and keep a basic account. What do you do?
results.answer:
I'd probably opt out and keep the basic account. CHF 5 per month might not seem like a lot, but for me, it's about being mindful of where my money goes, and I just don't see the added value of a Visa card over my current setup, especially since I mainly use Twint for everyday purchases and payments. Sticking with what I have saves me CHF 60 a year, which could go towards something I actually need. [/ANS]

results.question: A new Visa card offers 1% cashback on all Migros and Coop purchases. The monthly fee is CHF 4. Would this change how you pay at the supermarket?
results.answer:
Honestly, I'm not sure. While the idea of getting 1% cashback sounds good, the CHF 4 monthly fee translates to CHF 48 a year. To break even, I'd have to spend at least CHF 4,800 at Migros and Coop annually, which doesn't seem unrealistic given that those are my go-to places for groceries. However, considering my current habit of using Twint for these purchases, I'd have to weigh whether the convenience and potential cashback outweigh the cost and hassle of potentially needing to manage another card. Right now, I'm inclined to stick with what I know and avoid adding another expense to my budget. [/ANS]

results.question: You currently use Twint for almost everything. A Visa card promises the same speed but adds rewards. What would it take for you to actually switch?
results.answer:
Honestly, it would take some pretty compelling rewards for me to consider switching from Twint. I mean, Twint has been reliable and convenient, and I've gotten used to splitting bills and paying with it seamlessly. If a Visa card could offer, say, a guaranteed 1% to 2% cashback on all purchases, with no strings attached and no annual fee, that might catch my attention. But it would also depend on how easily I could integrate it into my existing routine and whether it supports all the merchants I usually visit. Convenience and simplicity are key for me, so any new card would have to fit neatly into my lifestyle without complicating things. [/ANS]

results.question: If a Visa card saved you CHF 15/month through cashback and discounts, but cost CHF 10/month in fees, would you see that as a net gain or still feel reluctant?
results.answer:
I think I would see it as a net gain, but my enthusiasm would be tempered. Saving CHF 5 per month (CHF 15 in benefits minus CHF 10 in fees) does amount to CHF 60 over a year, which is nothing to sneeze at for someone on a tight budget like myself. However, I'd still want to consider the hassle factor - would I need to change my spending habits significantly to achieve those savings? Are there any conditions or limits to the cashback and discounts that might reduce their actual value? Generally, though, if it's genuinely effortless to save that money, I'd consider it a decent proposition. [/ANS]

results.question: If a Visa card were completely free forever but offered no rewards, would you still get one? What would be the point for you?
results.answer:
Honestly, I'm not sure I'd get one even if it were completely free. Since it doesn't offer any rewards or benefits beyond what I already have with Twint and my debit card, the main advantage would be the ability to use it places that don't accept Twint or my debit card. However, most places I go to do accept my current methods of payment, so the incentive isn't strong enough for me to sign up for another card. Unless there was a specific, practical benefit - like being able to earn cashback, build credit, or get exclusive discounts somewhere I regularly shop - I don't see a compelling reason to add another card to my wallet. [/ANS]
